newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left win would hit PIBOR hard - survey.
newsitem.headline: French left win would hit PIBOR hard - survey.

text.p: A win for the opposition left in Sunday's French parliamentary election would knock another 30 basis points off June PIBOR but the long-term impact would be limited, according to a Reuter survey of economists on Thursday.

The median forecast for June PIBOR after a win for the left was 95.95, implying three-month rates of 4.05 percent, compared with 96.27 on Thursday, despite the fact more and more people are betting on change of government.
But by October 15, the 12 economists surveyed predicted the PIBOR future would recover to 96.38 if the left won, or 96.65 if the centre-right coalition retained power.

The franc would rally two centimes if the right pulled off a late recovery and slide to 3.40 per mark from just below 3.38 now if the opposition left held onto its first round lead, the survey showed.
Since a previous poll on May 7, several economists have toned down their predictions for French market underperformance versus Germany at the front of the bond yield curve in the event of a left win.
The median forecast for the two-year spread in October was 10 basis points compared with 25 basis points on May 7.
Similarly, economists expected French and German 10-year yields to be at the same level by October if the left won. Three weeks ago they predicted French yields would be above German yields.

Some economists said the fact Germany was facing similar deficit and unemployment problems as France meant the franc would probably return to the same level against the mark whichever party won on Sunday.
Francois Chevallier, economist at BFCE, predicted the French franc would be at 3.3550 per mark by mid October in the event of a right or a left victory.

"Germany is as ill as France is, this is the great difference with the previous elections, we have nothing to ask of the Germans," he said. "If something happens, people will sell francs and marks against the dollar. The franc and the mark are closely linked."
